title: Matrices in Machine Learning
description: Transpose and special matrices, solving linear systems, and the eigenvectors behind dimensionality reduction

lessons.title: Transpose & Special Matrices
lessons.description: Flip a matrix with transpose, and recognize the identity, diagonal, and symmetric matrices you'll see everywhere

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Transpose a matrix, and recognize identity, diagonal, and symmetric matrices.

sections.title: 🔃 Transpose: flipping rows and columns
sections.content:
The **transpose** of a matrix flips it over its diagonal — rows become columns, and columns become rows. Written as `Mᵀ` (or `M.T` in code):

```python
M = np.array([
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
])
print(M.T)
# [[1 4]
#  [2 5]
#  [3 6]]
print(M.T.shape)   # (3, 2) — rows and columns swap
```

Transpose shows up constantly when shapes don't line up for multiplication — flipping one matrix is often exactly what's needed to make two matrices compatible.

sections.title: 🪞 The identity matrix: 'do nothing'
sections.content:
The **identity matrix** has 1s down its diagonal and 0s everywhere else. Multiplying anything by it changes nothing — it's the matrix equivalent of multiplying a number by 1:

```python
I = np.eye(3)
print(I)
# [[1. 0. 0.]
#  [0. 1. 0.]
#  [0. 0. 1.]]
v = np.array([7, 8, 9])
print(I @ v)   # [7. 8. 9.] — unchanged
```

sections.title: 🔷 Diagonal and symmetric matrices
sections.content:
Two more shapes worth recognizing on sight:

• A **diagonal matrix** has numbers only on its diagonal, zeros everywhere else — like the identity, but the diagonal values can be anything (this is exactly the stretching matrix from the previous module's matrix-vector example)
• A **symmetric matrix** is unchanged by transpose — `M == Mᵀ` — meaning it's mirror-symmetric across its diagonal

You'll meet symmetric matrices again very soon: a matrix's own transpose multiplied by itself (`Mᵀ @ M`) is always symmetric, and that pattern is the foundation of the next lesson.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting that transposing changes a matrix's shape, not just its layout — a (2, 3) matrix becomes (3, 2). Assuming every matrix is symmetric — most aren't; symmetry is a special property worth noticing when it does hold.

questions.question: If M has shape (4, 7), what is the shape of M.T?
options: (4, 7) — unchanged
questions.explanation: Transpose swaps rows and columns, so a (4, 7) matrix becomes (7, 4) after transposing.

questions.question: What does multiplying any vector by the identity matrix produce?
options: The zero vector
A vector with every element doubled
The exact same vector, unchanged
A vector of a different shape
questions.explanation: The identity matrix is the multiplicative 'do nothing' matrix — multiplying by it leaves any vector exactly as it was.

questions.question: What defines a symmetric matrix?
options: It only contains positive numbers
It equals its own transpose (M == Mᵀ)
It has the same number of rows and columns as the identity matrix
All of its entries are zero except the diagonal
questions.explanation: A symmetric matrix is mirror-symmetric across its diagonal, meaning transposing it produces the exact same matrix.

questions.question: If you take the transpose of a matrix twice ((Mᵀ)ᵀ), what do you get?
options: A matrix of zeros
The original matrix M, unchanged
The identity matrix
A matrix with double the values
questions.explanation: Transposing twice swaps rows and columns back to their original arrangement, returning the original matrix M.

questions.question: What defines a diagonal matrix?
options: Every entry is the same value
All entries are zero except possibly those on the main diagonal
It must be the identity matrix
It has more rows than columns
questions.explanation: A diagonal matrix has non-zero values only along its main diagonal, with zeros everywhere else.

questions.question: How does transposing a product of two matrices work: (AB)ᵀ = ?
options: Aᵀ Bᵀ
Bᵀ Aᵀ
AB, unchanged
It cannot be computed
questions.explanation: The transpose of a product reverses the order of the factors and transposes each: (AB)ᵀ = Bᵀ Aᵀ.

questions.question: Why do covariance matrices in statistics and ML tend to be symmetric?
options: They're never actually symmetric
Because the covariance between variable X and Y is the same whether computed as (X,Y) or (Y,X)
Because they're always diagonal matrices
Because they only contain positive numbers
questions.explanation: Covariance between two variables doesn't depend on the order you name them, so the resulting matrix is naturally symmetric (equal to its own transpose).

questions.question: How is the transpose used when computing a dot product via matrix notation, like xᵀy?
options: It's not used for dot products
Writing xᵀy turns two column vectors into a matrix multiplication that produces the same result as the dot product
It reverses the order of the elements in x
It only works when x and y have different lengths
questions.explanation: Representing vectors as columns, xᵀy reshapes x into a row so the matrix multiplication xᵀy computes exactly the same scalar as the dot product x · y.

lessons.title: Systems of Linear Equations
lessons.description: See Ax = b as many equations at once, and solve a small system

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Recognize a system of equations written as Ax = b, and solve a small system in code.

sections.title: 📋 Many equations, one matrix expression
sections.content:
A **system of linear equations** is just several equations that need to be true at the same time. Written out:

```text
2x + y = 8
 x - y = 1
```

This exact system can be written compactly as `Ax = b`, using a matrix `A`, an unknown vector `x`, and a result vector `b`:

```python
A = np.array([
    [2, 1],
    [1, -1],
])
b = np.array([8, 1])
```

This isn't just notation — it's the exact same matrix-vector multiplication from Module 0. Solving 'find x' means finding the vector that, multiplied by A, produces b.

sections.title: 🧮 Solving with NumPy
sections.content:
You almost never solve these by hand — `np.linalg.solve` does it directly:

```python
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x)   # [3. 2.]
```

Check it: `2*3 + 2 = 8` ✓ and `3 - 2 = 1` ✓ — both original equations hold with x = [3, 2]. This same idea, scaled up to thousands of variables, is exactly what's happening under the hood when a linear regression model is fit to data.

sections.title: 💡 Why this matters for AI
sections.content: Linear regression's classic 'closed form' solution is literally solving a linear system: given a matrix of features and a vector of target values, you're solving for the weight vector that best explains the data. You don't need to solve these by hand — the point is recognizing that `Ax = b` is the mathematical shape underneath a huge amount of machine learning.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Trying to solve a system where A isn't a square matrix with np.linalg.solve directly — that function expects a square, well-behaved system; non-square systems need different tools (least squares), which is beyond this lesson's scope but good to know exists.

questions.question: What does the equation Ax = b represent?
options: A single equation with one unknown
A system of multiple linear equations, written compactly using a matrix and vectors
A rule for multiplying two matrices together
A way to compute a vector's length
questions.explanation: Ax = b packages a whole system of linear equations into one matrix expression: A holds the coefficients, x holds the unknowns, and b holds the results each equation must equal.

questions.question: What does np.linalg.solve(A, b) return?
options: The transpose of A
The vector x that satisfies Ax = b
The identity matrix
The sum of A's rows
questions.explanation: It solves the system for the unknown vector x — the values that, when multiplied by A, produce exactly b.

questions.question: How does linear regression relate to solving a system of linear equations?
options: It's unrelated to linear algebra
Fitting a linear regression model is essentially solving for the weight vector in a system built from the feature matrix and target values
Linear regression only works with a single feature, so systems never apply
Linear regression requires a symmetric matrix
questions.explanation: Linear regression's classic solution finds the weight vector that best satisfies a system built from the data — the exact same Ax = b shape covered in this lesson, just at a much larger scale.

questions.question: For Ax = b to have a unique solution, what does A typically need to be?
options: Any matrix, regardless of shape
Square and invertible
A vector, not a matrix
Symmetric only
questions.explanation: A unique solution generally requires A to be square (same number of equations as unknowns) and invertible — otherwise there may be no solution or infinitely many.

questions.question: What does it mean if matrix A in Ax = b is singular (non-invertible)?
options: The system always has exactly one solution
The system may have no solution or infinitely many, rather than a single unique one
x must always equal zero
np.linalg.solve will run faster
questions.explanation: A singular matrix means A doesn't have a well-defined inverse, so the system Ax = b can fail to have a unique solution.

questions.question: What's the difference between an overdetermined and underdetermined system of equations?
options: They're the same thing
Overdetermined has more equations than unknowns; underdetermined has fewer equations than unknowns
Overdetermined always has no solution
Underdetermined always has a unique solution
questions.explanation: Overdetermined systems have more constraints (equations) than unknowns, often leading to no exact solution, while underdetermined systems have fewer equations than unknowns, often leading to infinitely many solutions.

questions.question: Geometrically, what does solving a 2-variable system of 2 linear equations represent?
options: Finding the area under a curve
Finding the point where two lines intersect
Finding the slope of a single line
Computing a vector's length
questions.explanation: Each linear equation in two variables represents a line, and solving the system means finding the (x, y) point where those lines cross.

questions.question: How do the 'normal equations' in linear regression connect to solving Ax = b?
options: They're unrelated to systems of equations
The optimal regression weights can be found by solving a system of linear equations derived from the data (the normal equations)
Linear regression never uses matrix algebra
The normal equations only apply to classification problems
questions.explanation: The closed-form solution to linear regression comes from solving a linear system (the normal equations) built from the feature matrix and target values.

lessons.title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors
lessons.description: Find the special directions a matrix doesn't rotate — only stretches

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what an eigenvector and eigenvalue are, and compute them for a small matrix in code.

sections.title: 🎯 Directions a matrix leaves alone
sections.content:
Recall from Module 0 that a matrix transforms vectors — usually rotating and stretching them. For most matrices, there are a few special directions where the matrix **only stretches, and doesn't rotate at all**. Those special directions are **eigenvectors**, and the amount they get stretched by is the matching **eigenvalue**.

```text
M @ v = λ * v
```

In words: multiplying eigenvector `v` by matrix `M` gives back the exact same direction, just scaled by the number `λ` (lambda), the eigenvalue.

sections.title: 🧮 Finding them with NumPy
sections.content:
```python
M = np.array([
    [2, 0],
    [0, 3],
])
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(M)
print(eigenvalues)    # [2. 3.]
print(eigenvectors)
# [[1. 0.]
#  [0. 1.]]
```

For this diagonal matrix, the eigenvectors are just the x and y axes — matching exactly how this matrix stretches x by 2 and y by 3, which is the same example from Module 0's matrix-vector lesson.

sections.title: 💡 Why eigenvectors matter in AI
sections.content:
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues answer the question: **what are the most important directions in this data or transformation, and how strong is each one?**

• In dimensionality reduction (PCA, next lesson), the eigenvectors of a dataset's covariance matrix reveal the directions of greatest variation
• A large eigenvalue means that direction matters a lot; a small one means it barely matters and can often be dropped

You won't compute eigenvalues by hand in practice — libraries do it — but recognizing 'this is looking for the important directions in the data' is the intuition worth keeping.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Expecting every matrix's eigenvectors to be as clean as the diagonal example above — for most matrices, they point in less obvious directions. Confusing an eigenvalue (a single number, the amount of stretch) with an eigenvector (the direction itself) — they're always found in matching pairs.

questions.question: In M @ v = λ * v, what does this equation say about v?
options: v is transformed into a completely different direction by M
v's direction is unchanged by M — it's only scaled by the factor λ
v must be the zero vector
M and v must have the same shape
questions.explanation: This is the defining eigenvector equation: applying M to v produces a vector pointing in the exact same direction as v, just scaled by λ — no rotation.

questions.question: What does a large eigenvalue typically indicate?
options: That direction is unimportant and can be safely ignored
That direction is stretched a lot by the matrix — it captures a lot of variation or importance
The matrix is not invertible
The matrix must be symmetric
questions.explanation: A large eigenvalue means the matrix stretches that particular direction by a large amount, which is why large eigenvalues are associated with directions of high variance or importance in data.

questions.question: Why are eigenvectors relevant to dimensionality reduction?
options: They're unrelated to dimensionality reduction
The eigenvectors of a dataset's covariance matrix reveal the directions where the data varies the most, which is exactly what techniques like PCA use to compress data
Eigenvectors only apply to square images
They're used only to solve systems of linear equations
questions.explanation: Dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA rely on eigenvectors to find the directions of greatest variation in the data, keeping the ones with the largest eigenvalues and dropping the rest.

questions.question: For an n×n matrix, how many eigenvalues does it typically have (counting repeats)?
options: Exactly 1
Exactly n
n squared
It varies randomly
questions.explanation: An n×n matrix has exactly n eigenvalues, though some may repeat or be complex numbers.

questions.question: What does a negative eigenvalue mean for its corresponding eigenvector?
options: The eigenvector's direction flips (points opposite) when transformed by the matrix, in addition to being scaled
The eigenvector becomes the zero vector
The matrix has no real eigenvectors
It's mathematically impossible
questions.explanation: A negative eigenvalue means the transformation flips the eigenvector's direction while still scaling its length by the eigenvalue's magnitude.

questions.question: Why are eigenvectors often normalized to unit length in practice?
options: It's required by the definition of an eigenvector
So that only the direction matters and different eigenvectors can be fairly compared, since any scaled version of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector
Because unnormalized eigenvectors are always wrong
To make eigenvalues equal to 1
questions.explanation: Since any scalar multiple of an eigenvector is still an eigenvector, normalizing to unit length gives a consistent, comparable representation of just the direction.

questions.question: Why is it useful that symmetric matrices (like covariance matrices) always have real eigenvalues?
options: It isn't useful — real eigenvalues cause problems
It guarantees techniques like PCA, which rely on covariance matrices, produce meaningful, real-valued directions of variation instead of complex numbers
It means the matrix must be diagonal
It only matters for non-square matrices
questions.explanation: Because covariance matrices are symmetric, their eigenvalues and eigenvectors are guaranteed to be real numbers, which is essential for PCA's directions of variation to make practical sense.

questions.question: What is the general idea behind eigen-decomposition of a matrix?
options: Rewriting a matrix as the sum of two random matrices
Expressing a matrix in terms of its eigenvectors and eigenvalues, which reveals the fundamental directions and scaling it represents
Converting a matrix into a single scalar
Deleting all off-diagonal entries
questions.explanation: Eigen-decomposition breaks a matrix down into its eigenvectors and eigenvalues, exposing the core directions the matrix stretches or shrinks and by how much.

lessons.title: Dimensionality Reduction Intuition
lessons.description: See how keeping only the most important directions compresses data with minimal loss

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain the intuition behind PCA/SVD-style dimensionality reduction using eigenvectors.

sections.title: 📉 The problem: too many dimensions
sections.content: Real datasets often have dozens, hundreds, or thousands of features — dimensions. Many of those dimensions are redundant or barely matter, which makes data harder to visualize, slower to process, and can even hurt some models. **Dimensionality reduction** compresses data down to fewer dimensions while keeping as much of the meaningful information as possible.

sections.title: 🧭 The core idea: keep the important directions
sections.content:
This is where eigenvectors from the last lesson pay off directly. The recipe (this is the essence of **PCA**, Principal Component Analysis):

• Measure how the data varies across all its features (its **covariance**)
• Find the eigenvectors of that covariance — the directions of greatest spread
• Keep only the top few eigenvectors (the ones with the largest eigenvalues)
• Re-express each data point using just those few directions

You've just compressed the data — say, from 100 dimensions down to 2 — while discarding mostly redundant, low-variance information.

sections.title: 🖼️ A concrete mental picture
sections.content: Imagine data points scattered roughly along a diagonal line in 2D, with a little scatter perpendicular to it. The direction *along* the line is the top eigenvector — it captures almost all the spread. The direction *perpendicular* to it is a much smaller eigenvalue — mostly noise. Keeping only the first direction and dropping the second compresses each 2D point down to a single number, losing very little of what actually matters.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Assuming dimensionality reduction is lossless — it isn't; you're deliberately discarding the lowest-variance directions, trading a small amount of information for a much simpler representation. Applying it blindly without checking how much variance the kept dimensions actually retain.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind PCA-style dimensionality reduction?
options: Randomly delete some of the features
Find the directions of greatest variation (via eigenvectors) and keep only the most important ones
Always reduce every dataset down to exactly 2 dimensions
Replace all values with their average
questions.explanation: PCA identifies the eigenvectors of the data's covariance — the directions capturing the most spread — and keeps only the top ones, discarding lower-variance directions.

questions.question: In the 'diagonal scatter' example, why is the direction along the line kept and the perpendicular direction dropped?
options: The perpendicular direction is always exactly zero
The direction along the line has a much larger eigenvalue (captures much more of the data's spread) than the perpendicular direction
It's an arbitrary choice with no mathematical basis
Both directions are always kept in PCA
questions.explanation: The direction along the line corresponds to a large eigenvalue because most of the data's variation happens along it, while the perpendicular direction has a small eigenvalue since there's little spread that way — so it can be dropped with minimal information loss.

questions.question: Is dimensionality reduction lossless?
options: Yes, no information is ever lost
No — it deliberately discards the lowest-variance directions in exchange for a simpler representation
Only when reducing to exactly 1 dimension
Only when the original data has fewer than 10 dimensions
questions.explanation: Dimensionality reduction is a deliberate tradeoff: you keep the directions that matter most and accept a small loss of information from the directions you drop.

questions.question: Besides compressing data, what's another common reason to reduce dimensionality?
options: To make data impossible to visualize
To visualize high-dimensional data in 2D or 3D, or to reduce noise and computational cost
To increase the number of features
It has no other practical use
questions.explanation: Dimensionality reduction is also used to visualize otherwise-unplottable high-dimensional data and to cut down on noise and computation.

questions.question: How do practitioners commonly decide how many principal components to keep?
options: Always keep exactly 2, regardless of the data
By choosing enough components to retain a target percentage of the total explained variance
By keeping every component, since dropping any loses information
By flipping a coin
questions.explanation: A common approach is to keep enough top components so that their cumulative explained variance reaches a chosen threshold, like 95%.

questions.question: How do you apply a fitted PCA transformation to a brand-new data point?
options: Refit PCA from scratch using only that one point
Project it onto the same principal directions (eigenvectors) that were found from the original training data
It can't be done — PCA only works on the original dataset
Randomly assign it new coordinates
questions.explanation: A new point is projected onto the same eigenvector directions computed during training, keeping the transformation consistent.

questions.question: How does dimensionality reduction (like PCA) differ from feature selection?
options: They are exactly the same technique
PCA creates new combined directions from all original features, while feature selection simply chooses a subset of the original features to keep
Feature selection always outperforms PCA
PCA can only be applied to 2 features at a time
questions.explanation: PCA constructs new axes as combinations of the original features, whereas feature selection keeps some original features as-is and discards others entirely.

questions.question: Which specific matrix's eigenvectors does standard PCA rely on?
options: The identity matrix
The dataset's covariance matrix
A randomly generated matrix
The transpose of the raw data matrix only
questions.explanation: PCA computes the covariance matrix of the data and uses its eigenvectors as the new directions (principal components) to project onto.
